title: Fixed-Income (Debt) Securities
fullTitle: Types and Characteristics of Fixed-Income (Debt) Securities

los.text: Recognize the characteristics common to most bonds.
Identify the relevance of a bond's rating.
Calculate the price of a bond.
Calculate the parity price of a convertible bond.
Compare current yield, yield to maturity, and yield to call.
Recognize the unique features of U.S. government and agency issues.
Differentiate between secured and unsecured corporate debt.
Recall the unique features of municipal bonds, including the calculation of tax-equivalent yield.
Identify the advantages and disadvantages of investing in foreign debt securities.
Recall the methods of repayment of principal.
Identify the special characteristics of money market instruments and the risks and benefits of adding them to a client's portfolio.

concepts.explanation: A bond is a loan: the investor lends the issuer money for a set period at a fixed annual rate (the coupon). The contract is the indenture (deed of trust): amount due, maturity date, interest rate, any collateral. Three big issuers: the U.S. government (largest), corporations, and state/local governments (municipals). Governments issue only debt — you cannot own stock in the Treasury. Long-term debt is generally 5+ years, usually 10–30; money market instruments mature in one year or less.
rules: Interest is a contractual obligation (paid before any dividend); skipping it can mean bankruptcy — no company ever failed for skipping a dividend.
Corporate interest is a pre-tax expense (deductible); dividends are paid from after-tax income.
Bonds are negotiable (freely transferable) and have a specified maturity.
exceptions: Money market instruments are issued at a discount instead of paying periodic interest.
misconceptions: Treating bond interest like a dividend that can be skipped.

concepts.explanation: When market interest rates rise, prices of outstanding bonds fall; when rates fall, prices rise. That is interest-rate risk. The coupon payments themselves never change — only the price does. Interest is normally paid semiannually. A bond sold between payment dates trades 'and interest': the buyer pays the price plus the interest accrued since the last payment, then collects the full next coupon.
rules: Rates up → bond prices down; rates down → prices up.
Par value never changes with rates — only market price does.
Buyer pays seller accrued interest; buyer gets the whole next payment.
misconceptions: Saying par value rises when rates fall — par is fixed; market price rises.

concepts.subtopic: S&P and Moody's scales; investment grade vs. high yield
concepts.explanation: S&P and Moody's rate default (credit) risk. S&P: AAA, AA, A, BBB | BB, B, CCC, C (income bond paying no interest), D (default); Moody's: Aaa, Aa, A, Baa | Ba, B, Caa, Ca, C. The top four categories (BBB/Baa and above) are investment grade — generally the only quality institutions and fiduciaries may buy, so they are more liquid. BB/Ba and below are high-yield ('junk'): higher default risk, more volatile, higher return to compensate (risk–reward). S&P uses + and −; Moody's uses 1, 2, 3 within Aa through B. Raters consider everything, including collateral — a mortgage bond is not automatically safer than a debenture. A rating 'under review' usually signals concern about the issuer's ability to perform.
rules: Investment grade = BBB/Baa or higher (top four).
Lower rating → higher yield required.
Think of ratings as the borrower's credit score.
exceptions: A strong issuer's unsecured debenture can be safer than a weak issuer's secured mortgage bond.
examples: S&P top four best-to-lowest: AAA, AA, A, BBB. Moody's: Aaa, Aa, A, Baa.
misconceptions: Mixing the two scales (e.g., listing Aaa as an S&P grade).
Thinking A is below BBB.

concepts.subtopic: Price quotes: corporates/munis in eighths, Treasuries in 32nds
concepts.explanation: Par is always $1,000. Corporate and municipal bonds are quoted as a percent of par in points ($10) and eighths ($1.25): 90 1/4 = $902.50; 101 3/4 = $1,017.50. Treasury quotes use 32nds: the digits after the decimal are 32nds of a point ($0.3125 each): 90.8 (or 90.08) = 90 8/32 = $902.50; 101.24 = $1,017.50; 104.16 = $1,045. A listing like 'DEF 5s35 @106' means issuer DEF, 5% coupon, matures 2035, price $1,060 — the 's' just separates coupon from year.
rules: 1 point = $10; corporate fraction 1/8 = $1.25; Treasury .01 = 1/32 = $0.3125.
Convert Treasury decimals as 32nds, never as hundredths.
examples: 103 1/2 corporate = $1,035; the same price on a Treasury shows as 103.16.

concepts.explanation: Only corporations issue convertibles (usually debentures) because they convert into the issuer's common stock. Conversion ratio = $1,000 ÷ conversion price, fixed in the indenture; the bond's market price never changes the ratio. Parity means the bond and the shares it converts into are worth the same. Parity price of the stock = bond market price ÷ conversion ratio; parity price of the bond = conversion ratio × stock price. Percentage shortcut: if the bond is 20% above par, the parity stock price is 20% above the conversion price. In practice convertibles trade a bit above parity (the stock a bit below).
rules: Ratio = 1,000 ÷ conversion price — ignore the bond's current price.
Stock parity = bond price ÷ ratio; bond parity = ratio × stock price.
exceptions: No convertible municipal or government bonds exist.
formulas: Parity stock price = bond market price ÷ conversion ratio
Parity bond price = conversion ratio × stock market price
examples: Convertible at $50, bond at $1,200: ratio 20, parity stock = $60.
Convertible at $50, stock at $45: parity bond = 20 × 45 = $900.
misconceptions: Dividing the bond's market price by the conversion price to get shares (1,200 ÷ 40 = 30 is wrong; it is 1,000 ÷ 40 = 25).

concepts.explanation: Nominal yield (coupon rate) is fixed as a percent of par: a 5% bond pays $50 a year, paid semiannually ($25 twice) — '6% paid semiannually' means $60 a year in two $30 payments, not two $60 payments. Current yield = annual interest ÷ current market price (for stock: annual dividend ÷ price). A $100 coupon on a bond priced at $800 is a 12.5% CY; at $1,200 it is 8.33%. Pay more, get less; pay less, get more.
rules: Coupon dollars never change; current yield changes with price.
Discount → CY above coupon; premium → CY below coupon; par → equal.
formulas: Current yield = annual interest (or dividend) ÷ current market price
misconceptions: Doubling the coupon when a question says 'paid semiannually'.
Using par instead of market price in the denominator.

concepts.subtopic: Yield to maturity, yield to call, yield ranking
concepts.explanation: Yield to maturity (basis, the 'true' or market-driven yield, an IRR) adds the gain to par on a discount bond or subtracts the loss on a premium bond, spread over the years to maturity, and divides by the average price. So on a discount bond YTM > CY > nominal; on a premium bond YTM < CY < nominal; at par all are equal. Yield to call assumes early redemption at the call price, which accelerates a premium bond's loss, so YTC is the lowest yield on a premium bond and the highest on a discount bond (issuers rarely call discount bonds). Ranking lowest→highest — Discount: nominal, CY, YTM, YTC. Premium: YTC, YTM, CY, nominal. A bond always matures at par, so the purchase price alone tells you whether there is a gain or loss at maturity.
rules: Discount bond: nominal < CY < YTM < YTC.
Premium bond: YTC < YTM < CY < nominal.
Yield above coupon → discount; yield below coupon → premium.
YTC matters most for a premium callable bond.
exceptions: If a discount bond were called, YTC would exceed YTM because the gain is accelerated.
formulas: Approx. YTM = [annual interest ± (discount or premium ÷ years)] ÷ average price
misconceptions: Assuming YTM is always higher than CY — only true for discount bonds.

concepts.explanation: 'Government' on the exam means federal. Treasury issues carry the direct full-faith-and-credit guarantee; agency issues carry a moral guarantee. T-bills: short-term (4, 13, 26 weeks weekly; 52 weeks every four weeks), issued and traded at a discount, no stated interest rate (the only Treasury without one), highly liquid, book entry; the 13-week (91-day) bill is the 'risk-free' rate. T-notes: 2–10 years; T-bonds: 10–30 years; both pay semiannual interest, mature at par, are noncallable. All are book entry; denominations as low as $100, but exam math always uses $1,000 par. A falling T-bill auction yield means buyers paid more (prices up).
rules: T-bills: discount, no coupon, ≤ 1 year.
Notes 2–10 yrs, bonds 10–30 yrs; semiannual interest; noncallable.
Treasury interest: federally taxable, exempt from state and local tax.
examples: Buy a $10,000 26-week bill for $9,800; receive $10,000 at maturity; the $200 is interest income.
misconceptions: Thinking T-bills carry coupons.
Reading a lower auction yield as a lower price.

concepts.explanation: Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities carry a fixed rate but the principal is adjusted semiannually by the change in the CPI; each interest payment = fixed rate × adjusted principal, so payments rise with inflation and fall with deflation. Maturities 5, 10, 30 years. They pay a lower coupon than regular Treasuries. Taxes: interest and the annual principal increase are federally taxable in the year of adjustment (even though the increase is not received until maturity) but exempt from state and local tax. TIPS = periodic income + safety + purchasing-power protection.
rules: Principal adjusts with CPI; coupon rate is fixed.
Upward principal adjustments are taxable federally each year (phantom income).
formulas: TIPS payment = fixed rate × inflation-adjusted principal
misconceptions: Thinking the coupon rate rises with inflation — the principal does.

concepts.subtopic: GNMA, agencies (Fannie Mae), TVA, mortgage-backed risks
concepts.explanation: Ginnie Mae (GNMA) is a wholly owned government corporation whose modified pass-through certificates are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S.; they represent pools of FHA/VA mortgages, pay monthly (not semiannually), and each payment is part interest (taxable at all levels) and part principal; minimum $1,000. Government-sponsored enterprises such as Fannie Mae are only moral obligations (second in safety to Treasuries); Fannie Mae buys FHA/VA mortgages, issues bonds at par paying semiannual interest taxable at all levels, and its stock trades publicly. TVA bonds are backed by project revenues, not the government, though raters see an implicit guarantee. Mortgage-backed securities pay more than similarly rated debt but carry prepayment risk (homeowners refinance when rates fall → principal returns early → reinvest at lower rates; a form of reinvestment risk), default risk (subprime), complexity, and liquidity risk.
rules: GNMA = direct government backing; agencies (GSEs) = moral obligation.
GNMA pays monthly interest + principal.
Agency/GNMA interest is taxable at federal, state and local levels (unlike Treasuries).
misconceptions: Assuming all federal-sounding issuers have the full-faith guarantee — only Treasuries and GNMA do.

concepts.subtopic: Secured debt: mortgage bonds, equipment trust certificates, collateral trust bonds
concepts.explanation: Secured corporate debt is backed by specific pledged assets. Mortgage bonds: real estate and physical plant; if foreclosure proceeds fall short, the holder becomes a general creditor for the balance. Equipment trust certificates: rolling stock, locomotives, airplanes (railroads, airlines) — the company makes a down payment (~20%), pays the loan down as equipment depreciates, and gets title from the trustee when paid off. Collateral trust bonds (certificates): marketable securities deposited in trust — the better the securities, the better the rating.
rules: Three secured types: mortgage bonds, equipment trust certificates, collateral trust bonds.
Interest on all debt, secured or not, is paid before any dividend.
misconceptions: Counting a guaranteed bond as secured — a third-party promise is not a pledged asset of the issuer.

concepts.explanation: Debentures are backed only by the issuer's general credit (a corporate IOU); a strong issuer's debentures can be safer than a weak issuer's mortgage bonds. Guaranteed bonds are backed by a company other than the issuer (e.g., a parent guaranteeing a subsidiary) — worth only as much as the guarantor. Subordinated debentures rank behind all other creditors but still ahead of every stockholder. Liquidation priority: secured creditors → unsecured/general creditors (debentures) → subordinated debt → preferred stock → common stock. 'Senior securities' = bonds and preferred (senior to common); 'senior bonds' = secured bonds.
rules: Priority: secured → unsecured → subordinated → preferred → common.
Every debt security is senior to every stock.
misconceptions: Placing subordinated debentures below preferred stock — no debt ranks below equity.

concepts.explanation: Municipal securities are issued by states and political subdivisions (cities, counties, school districts). Their safety record is second only to Treasuries, and some issues are insured. General obligation (GO) bonds are backed by the issuer's full faith and credit, usually including unlimited ad valorem (property) taxes — analyzed by the tax base. Revenue bonds are paid from the earnings of a revenue-producing facility (water, sewer, toll bridge, airport, dorm) or lease rentals, often through an authority; they yield more than GOs because taxes are more secure than revenues.
rules: Ad valorem taxes back GOs; facility revenues back revenue bonds.
Revenue bonds generally yield more than GOs.
misconceptions: Attributing property-tax backing to corporate or Treasury debt — only municipalities levy them.

concepts.explanation: Corporate bond interest is taxed federally and by states; Treasury interest only federally; municipal interest is generally free of federal tax and, for residents of the issuing state, state tax too (double exemption raises the effective TEY). Tax-equivalent yield = municipal yield ÷ (1 − tax bracket): what a taxable bond must pay to match the muni after tax. Reverse: taxable yield × (1 − bracket) = the tax-free yield that is equivalent. Compare after-tax yields across choices to pick the best.
rules: TEY = muni coupon ÷ (100% − bracket).
After-tax taxable yield = coupon × (1 − bracket).
Use the federal bracket unless told the bond is also state-exempt.
exceptions: Higher bracket → munis more attractive; low-bracket investors often do better with taxables.
formulas: Equivalent tax-free yield = taxable yield × (1 − tax rate)
examples: 8% taxable at 30%: keeps 5.6%, so a 5.6% muni is equivalent.
misconceptions: Multiplying the muni yield by the bracket instead of dividing by the complement.

concepts.subtopic: Sovereign/foreign corporate bonds, Eurobonds, Eurodollar, Yankee, Brady
concepts.explanation: Foreign bonds (e.g., UK gilts, emerging-market sovereigns, foreign corporates) offer potentially higher returns, diversification, and a hedge against a falling dollar, with currency risk, higher default risk, less liquidity and higher trading costs. A Eurobond is issued outside the country of its currency and pays in foreign currency; a Eurodollar bond is issued outside the U.S. but pays in U.S. dollars (issuers include foreign and domestic corporations and governments, but never the U.S. Treasury). A Yankee bond is dollar-denominated, issued by a non-U.S. entity inside the U.S. market (Maple = Canadian version). Euro/Yankee issues avoid SEC registration (lower cost, less transparency) and yield more. Eurodollar advantages to U.S. investors: no currency risk, rated by U.S. agencies, higher yields; disadvantages: no SEC registration, political/country risk, less liquidity — and currency risk for non-U.S. holders. Brady bonds (1989 plan, Mexico first) restructured defaulted emerging-market bank loans into mostly dollar-denominated bonds often collateralized by U.S. Treasury zeros; safer and more liquid than other emerging-market debt, interest fully taxable, no U.S. government guarantee.
rules: Eurodollar bond: outside U.S., pays USD. Eurobond: pays foreign currency.
Yankee bond: USD, non-U.S. issuer, sold in the U.S.
Brady bonds: no U.S. guarantee; taxable interest.
exceptions: A French resident holding Eurodollar bonds does bear currency risk — only U.S. investors are free of it.
examples: £100,000 of 4% gilts always pay £4,000; if the pound falls from $1.41 to $1.25, the dollar value of principal drops from $141,000 to $125,000.
misconceptions: Calling a Eurodollar bond 'registered with the SEC' or 'guaranteed'.

concepts.explanation: Zero-coupon bonds pay no interest; they are issued at a deep discount and mature at par. Key facts: always issued at a discount; no reinvestment risk (nothing to reinvest); more volatile than coupon bonds of the same quality (lowest coupon + longest maturity = most volatile); taxed annually on imputed interest reported on Form 1099-OID — 'phantom income'. Ideal for a known future goal (college, retirement plans, where the phantom-income tax is avoided). Corporate and municipal zeros carry extra credit risk (nothing received until maturity); Treasury STRIPS have no credit risk (and are unrated because none is needed). Zeros lock in a yield for a chosen period.
rules: Zeros: discount, no reinvestment risk, high volatility, phantom income.
Safest zero for a long-dated goal: a Treasury STRIP.
examples: Pay $500 today for $1,000 in 10 years — $500 profit, about $50 a year, no checks along the way.
misconceptions: Thinking zeros avoid tax until maturity (outside a tax-advantaged account they do not).

concepts.subtopic: Callable bonds, refunding, call protection; convertibles as a hybrid
concepts.explanation: A call feature lets the issuer redeem bonds before maturity, usually when rates have fallen — it issues new lower-coupon bonds and retires the old (refunding, like refinancing). The call price is usually a premium to par, and after the final tender date interest and conversion rights end. Issuers do not call bonds trading at a discount — buying them in the open market is cheaper. Call protection = years before the first call; noncallable is the best protection. Convertible debentures are a hybrid: downside protection as a creditor (interest and principal are owed), upside tied to the common, lower coupon than nonconvertibles, less volatile than the stock, mitigates interest-rate risk — but they can be called before you convert. Antidilution: on a split or stock dividend the conversion ratio rises (price falls) so the holder keeps equivalent conversion power.
rules: Calls happen when rates fall; the holder bears reinvestment risk.
Noncallable = maximum call protection.
Convertible: creditor's safety + stockholder's upside, paid for with a lower coupon.
exceptions: Some allocators treat convertibles as equity rather than fixed income.
examples: Bond convertible into 20 shares; 2-for-1 split → convertible into 40 shares (conversion price halves).
misconceptions: Confusing who exercises: the issuer calls; the investor converts.

concepts.subtopic: Money market instruments: T-bills, negotiable CDs, commercial paper, Eurodollars, benchmark rates
concepts.explanation: The money market trades short-term loanable funds — instruments maturing in one year or less (most under six months), generally issued at a discount, all low risk. Buyer = lender; seller = borrower. T-bills (and Treasury notes/bonds in their final year) dominate. Negotiable (jumbo) CDs: unsecured bank time deposits of $100,000+ (often $1 million+), tradable before maturity, no prepayment penalty, FDIC-insured to $250,000, the one money market instrument issued at par and paying periodic (semiannual) interest. Commercial paper: short-term unsecured corporate notes (often finance companies) for working capital, issued at a discount, exempt from registration if maturity ≤ 270 days. Eurodollars: dollar deposits in banks outside the U.S. (Euroyen = yen outside Japan), typically overnight to 180 days, historically priced off LIBOR. Benefits of money market holdings: liquidity, safety, parking money needed soon. Risks: low returns (unsuitable as a long-term core) and fluctuating income on reinvestment.
rules: Money market = maturity ≤ 1 year.
Jumbo CDs: issued at par, pay interest, unsecured, no prepayment penalty.
Commercial paper: discount, unsecured, ≤ 270 days for exemption.
exceptions: Jumbo CDs are the exception to 'issued at a discount'.
examples: A company with cash it needs in 4–6 months belongs in T-bills, not stocks or long bonds.
misconceptions: Thinking negotiable CDs are secured by bank assets — they are unsecured deposits.

concepts.explanation: The book describes LIBOR (London Interbank Offered Rate), set daily in London from a survey of banks across 15 periods and several currencies, as the world's most widely used short-term benchmark, and notes it was scheduled to end June 30, 2023. EXTERNAL UPDATE: LIBOR publication did end (the final USD settings ceased in 2023, with a short synthetic tail into 2024). The main U.S. replacement is SOFR, the Secured Overnight Financing Rate — a broad measure of the cost of borrowing cash overnight collateralized by Treasury securities, published by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. If an exam question still names LIBOR, it is the London rate; if it asks about the current overnight Treasury-collateralized benchmark, that is SOFR.
rules: LIBOR = London, bank survey, discontinued.
SOFR = overnight, secured by Treasuries, published by the NY Fed.
misconceptions: Answering 'New York' for where LIBOR was set.

concepts.explanation: Cash in the bank is FDIC-insured up to legal limits. A demand deposit account (DDA) is the legal term for a checking account (today also savings and bank money market accounts — not money market mutual funds); withdrawable any time; safe, low return, short-term funds. Bank (nonnegotiable) CDs: minimum deposits as low as $500, 3 months to 5 years, early-withdrawal penalty, cannot be sold — only redeemed. For capital preservation with no risk, the answer is an insured bank CD: no interest-rate risk because it does not trade and its value does not fluctuate. Still liquid (less than a DDA). Risks: purchasing-power (inflation) risk and low yields.
rules: Insured bank CD / time deposit = no interest-rate risk.
DDA = checkbook access.
Money market mutual funds are securities, not bank deposits.
misconceptions: Picking a Treasury bond as 'no interest-rate risk' — it trades and fluctuates; a time deposit does not.

lessons.title: What a bond is, how its price moves, and what a rating means
lessons.objective: Describe the loan contract behind a bond, explain why prices move opposite to interest rates, handle accrued interest, and read S&P/Moody's ratings including the investment-grade line.

blocks.h: A bond is a loan with a contract
blocks.b:
Buy a bond and you have **lent** the issuer money for a fixed period at a fixed annual rate — the **coupon** (named for the detachable coupons bonds once carried). The contract is the **indenture** (deed of trust): how much is owed, when it matures, the interest rate, any collateral.

Three big borrowers: the **U.S. government** (the largest), **corporations**, and **states and their subdivisions** (municipal bonds). Governments can only issue debt — nobody owns stock in the Treasury.

Time frames: long-term debt is at least 5 years, usually **10–30**; **money market** instruments mature in **one year or less**.

blocks.h: Interest is an obligation, not a favor
blocks.b:
- Bond interest is normally paid **semiannually** and is a **contractual obligation**. Miss it and creditors can force bankruptcy. No company ever went bankrupt for skipping a dividend.
- For a corporation, interest is a **pre-tax, deductible expense**; dividends come out of after-tax income.
- Bonds are **negotiable** — you can sell before maturity, at whatever price the market gives you.
- Money market instruments skip coupons: they are sold at a **discount** and pay par at maturity.

When market interest rates **rise**, prices of existing bonds **fall**; when rates **fall**, prices **rise**. That is **interest-rate risk**. Two things never move: the **coupon payments** and the **par value**. Only the market price swings.

**Accrued interest**: sell between payment dates and the buyer pays you the price *plus* the interest earned since the last payment (trading 'and interest'). The buyer then keeps the full next coupon.

**Standard & Poor's** and **Moody's** grade default (credit) risk:

- S&P: **AAA, AA, A, BBB** | BB, B, CCC, C, D
- Moody's: **Aaa, Aa, A, Baa** | Ba, B, Caa, Ca, C

The top **four** categories (**BBB / Baa and higher**) are **investment grade** — generally the only quality institutions and fiduciaries may buy, so they are more liquid. Below that is **high-yield** (junk): more default risk, more volatility, and a higher return to compensate — the **risk–reward** relationship. S&P refines with + and −; Moody's with 1, 2, 3 (Aa through B). An S&P **C** is an income bond paying no interest; **D** is default.

Raters weigh everything, including collateral, so a **mortgage bond is not automatically safer than a debenture**. A rating 'under review' usually means concern about the issuer's ability to pay.

blocks.h: The two scales side by side

lessons.title: Bond math I: reading quotes and converting bonds
lessons.objective: Convert corporate/municipal and Treasury quotes into dollar prices, decode a bond listing, and compute conversion ratios and parity prices both ways.

blocks.b:
Par is always **$1,000**, and 1 point = 1% = **$10**.

**Corporate and municipal** bonds use **eighths**: each 1/8 = **$1.25**.
- 90 1/4 = $900 + $2.50 = **$902.50**
- 101 3/4 = $1,010 + $7.50 = **$1,017.50**

**Treasury** notes and bonds use **32nds**: the digits after the decimal are 32nds, each worth **$0.3125**.
- 90.8 (also written 90.08) = 90 8/32 = $900 + $2.50 = **$902.50**
- 101.24 = 101 24/32 = **$1,017.50**
- 104.16 = 104 16/32 = 104 1/2 = **$1,045** (not $1,041.60)

A listing such as **DEF 5s35 @106** reads: issuer DEF, **5%** coupon, matures **2035**, price **$1,060**. The 's' is just a separator.

blocks.h: Convertible bonds: the ratio is fixed at issue
blocks.b:
Only **corporations** issue convertibles (mostly debentures), because they convert into the issuer's **common stock** — so there are no convertible municipals or Treasuries. Conversion is the **investor's** choice.

The indenture states either the number of shares or a **conversion price**. Either way:

**Conversion ratio = $1,000 ÷ conversion price**

Convertible at $20 → 50 shares. At $50 → 20 shares. The bond's *current market price is irrelevant* — a bond selling at 120 convertible at $40 still converts into 25 shares, not 30.

blocks.h: Parity: when bond and shares are worth the same
blocks.b:
**Parity** means equal value between the bond and the stock you would get by converting.

- **Parity price of the stock** = bond market price ÷ conversion ratio
- **Parity price of the bond** = conversion ratio × stock market price

Percentage shortcut: a bond 20% above par implies a parity stock price 20% above the conversion price; a stock 10% below the conversion price implies a bond parity 10% below par.

In real markets convertibles usually trade a little **above** parity (equivalently, the stock a little below).

RST debenture convertible at $50; bond trades at $1,200. Ratio = 1,000 ÷ 50 = 20. Parity stock price = 1,200 ÷ 20 = **$60** (or: bond is up 20%, so 50 × 1.20 = 60).

Same bond, stock trading at $45: parity bond price = 20 × 45 = **$900** (stock is 10% below $50, so bond parity is 10% below $1,000).

lessons.title: Bond math II: the four yields and how they rank
lessons.objective: Compute current yield, explain yield to maturity and yield to call, and rank nominal, CY, YTM and YTC for discount and premium bonds.

blocks.b:
The **nominal yield** (coupon rate) is a fixed percent of **par**: a 5% bond pays **$50 a year**, as two $25 payments. Careful: '6% paid semiannually' means $60 a year in two $30 checks — *not* two $60 checks.

**Current yield = annual interest ÷ current market price.** (For a stock: annual dividend ÷ price. $2 dividend on a $40 stock = 5%.)

The $100 coupon on a 10% bond never changes, but:
- at **$800** the CY is 100 ÷ 800 = **12.5%** (discount → yield above coupon)
- at **$1,200** the CY is 100 ÷ 1,200 = **8.33%** (premium → yield below coupon)

**Pay more, get less. Pay less, get more.**

blocks.h: Yield to maturity: counting the gain or loss at par
blocks.b:
A bond **always matures at par**. Buy at a discount and you also get a **gain** at maturity; buy at a premium and you take a **loss**. **Yield to maturity** (YTM, 'basis', the true or market-driven yield — an internal rate of return) spreads that gain or loss over the years:

**Approx. YTM = [annual interest ± (discount or premium ÷ years)] ÷ average price**, where average price = (price paid + par) ÷ 2.

10% bond bought at 105 with 10 years left: (100 − 50 ÷ 10) ÷ 1,025 = 95 ÷ 1,025 ≈ **9.3%** — below the 9.52% CY and the 10% coupon.

10% bond bought at 95: (100 + 5) ÷ 975 ≈ **10.77%** — above the 10.53% CY and the 10% coupon.

You will see at most one YTM calculation; the **relationships** are what get tested.

blocks.h: Yield to call and the ranking
blocks.b:
**Yield to call** assumes the issuer redeems at the call date and call price. On a **premium** bond the loss is accelerated, so YTC is the **lowest** of the yields — the one a buyer of a premium callable bond must consider. Issuers rarely call discount bonds (cheaper to buy them back in the market); if they did, YTC would be the **highest** because the gain is accelerated.

**Ranking, lowest → highest**
- **Discount**: nominal < CY < YTM < YTC
- **Premium**: YTC < YTM < CY < nominal
- **Par**: all equal

Quick reads: yield above coupon → **discount**; yield below coupon → **premium**; YTM = CY → **par**; YTC lower than CY → **premium**; YTM lower than YTC → **discount**.

lessons.title: Treasuries, TIPS, Ginnie Mae and the agencies
lessons.objective: Distinguish T-bills, notes and bonds; explain how TIPS adjust and are taxed; and separate full-faith-and-credit issues (Treasuries, GNMA) from moral-obligation agencies, including mortgage-backed risks.

blocks.b:
On the exam, 'government' means **federal**, and Treasuries are the safest securities there are. Two kinds of backing exist: the **direct guarantee** (Treasuries, GNMA) and the **moral guarantee** (agencies).

- **T-bills**: short term — 4-, 13- and 26-week bills auctioned weekly, 52-week every four weeks. Issued and traded at a **discount**, **no stated interest rate** (the only Treasury without one), highly liquid. The **13-week (91-day) bill is the 'risk-free' rate**. When an auction yield *falls*, buyers *paid more*.
- **T-notes**: 2, 3, 5, 7, 10 years; semiannual interest; mature at par; **noncallable**.
- **T-bonds**: 10–30 years; same features.

All are **book entry** (no certificates), available in $100 pieces — but exam math always uses $1,000 par. Treasury interest is **federally taxable, exempt from state and local tax**.

blocks.h: TIPS: inflation protection with a tax wrinkle
blocks.b:
**Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities** pay a **fixed rate** on a **principal that adjusts semiannually with the CPI**. Payment = fixed rate × adjusted principal, so checks grow with inflation (and shrink with deflation). Maturities 5, 10, 30 years; lower coupon than regular Treasuries.

Tax: interest **and** each year's upward principal adjustment are **federally taxable that year** (phantom income — you don't receive the increase until maturity) but **exempt from state and local tax**.

Client wants periodic income + safety of principal + purchasing-power protection → **TIPS**.

**GNMA (Ginnie Mae)** is a wholly owned government corporation; its **modified pass-through certificates** carry the **full faith and credit of the U.S.** They represent pools of **FHA/VA mortgages**. Two quirks: payments arrive **monthly**, and each payment is **part interest, part principal**. Interest is taxable at **all** levels. Minimum $1,000.

**Government-sponsored enterprises** (e.g., **Fannie Mae**) are quasi-governmental: **moral obligations**, not guaranteed — second in safety to Treasuries. Fannie Mae buys FHA/VA mortgages, issues bonds at par with semiannual interest taxable at all levels, and its stock is publicly traded. **TVA** bonds are backed by project **revenues**, though raters assume an implicit guarantee.

**Mortgage-backed securities** pay more than similarly rated debt, but bring **prepayment risk** — homeowners refinance when rates fall, principal comes back early, and you reinvest at lower rates (a form of reinvestment risk) — plus default risk (subprime), complexity and liquidity risk.

lessons.title: Corporate debt: secured, unsecured, and who gets paid first
lessons.objective: Identify the three secured corporate bonds, explain debentures, guaranteed and subordinated bonds, and reproduce the liquidation priority.

blocks.b:
Secured debt is backed by **specific pledged assets** of the issuer.
- **Mortgage bonds** — real estate and physical plant. If foreclosure doesn't cover the balance, the holder becomes a general creditor for the rest.
- **Equipment trust certificates** — rolling stock, locomotives, airplanes (railroads, airlines). ~20% down, the loan is paid down as the equipment wears out, and the trustee hands over title at the end. Like a car loan.
- **Collateral trust bonds** (certificates) — marketable **securities** deposited in trust. Better collateral, better rating.

Whatever the backing, **interest on debt is paid before any dividend**.

- **Debentures** — backed only by the issuer's general credit; a corporate IOU. A blue-chip debenture can be safer than a shaky company's mortgage bond.
- **Guaranteed bonds** — a company *other than the issuer* guarantees interest (or interest and principal), e.g., a parent guaranteeing a pipeline subsidiary. Worth exactly as much as the guarantor. **Not** secured — no asset of the issuer is pledged.
- **Subordinated debentures** — rank behind every other creditor… but still **ahead of every stockholder**.

rows: Secured creditors: mortgage bonds, equipment trust certificates, collateral trust bonds

blocks.b: Preferred is senior to common; every bond is senior to preferred; secured bonds are senior to debentures. **Senior securities** = bonds and preferred stock (senior to common). If a question says a company issued **senior bonds**, it is talking about **secured** bonds — mortgage, collateral trust or equipment trust — with priority over unsecured creditors.

lessons.title: Municipal bonds and tax-equivalent yield
lessons.objective: Distinguish GO from revenue bonds, state how municipal, Treasury and corporate interest are taxed, and compute tax-equivalent yield in both directions.

blocks.b:
**Municipal securities** are debt of a state or its political subdivisions — city, county, school district. Their safety record is second only to Treasuries, and some issues are **insured** against missed payments.

- **General obligation (GO) bonds** — backed by the issuer's full faith and credit, usually including **unlimited ad valorem (property) taxes**. Analyze the tax base. Very safe.
- **Revenue bonds** — paid from the earnings of a revenue-producing facility (water, sewer, electric, toll bridge, airport, college dorm) or lease rentals, often via an authority. **Higher yield than GOs** — taxes are more secure than revenues.

- **Corporate** bond interest: taxed federally **and** by the states.
- **Treasury** interest: federal only.
- **Municipal** interest: generally **free of federal tax**, and free of **state tax too if you live in the issuing state** — the 'double exemption' that makes in-state munis worth more to residents.

**TEY = municipal yield ÷ (100% − tax bracket)** — what a taxable bond would have to pay to leave you the same after tax.

7.5% muni, 28% bracket: 7.5 ÷ 0.72 = **10.42%**. A 10% corporate nets only 7.2%, so the muni wins.
4.2% muni, 40% bracket: 4.2 ÷ 0.60 = **7%**. (Check: 7% − 40% tax = 4.2%.)

Reverse direction: taxable yield × (1 − bracket) = the muni yield that matches. An 8% taxable at 30% keeps 5.6%, so a **5.6%** muni is equivalent.

Highest-after-tax-yield questions: convert every taxable choice with × (1 − bracket) and compare with the muni as is.
37% bracket. Choices: 2.25% T-note → 1.42%; 3.75% T-bond → 2.36%; 5.25% corporate → 3.31%; 3.55% muni → 3.55%. The municipal bond gives the highest after-tax yield.

lessons.title: Foreign bonds: Eurobonds, Eurodollar, Yankee and Brady
lessons.objective: State the advantages and risks of foreign debt and tell apart Eurobonds, Eurodollar bonds, Yankee bonds and Brady bonds.

blocks.h: Why go abroad, and what it costs
blocks.b:
Foreign bonds range from very safe **UK gilts** to emerging-market sovereigns rated like junk, plus foreign corporates.

**Advantages**: potentially higher returns, diversification, a hedge against a falling U.S. dollar.
**Added risks**: **currency risk**, higher default risk, less liquidity, higher trading costs. Most investors reach them through mutual funds (Unit 3).

Currency risk in one picture: £100,000 of 4% gilts always pays £4,000. If the pound slides from $1.41 to $1.25, your $141,000 of bonds is worth $125,000 at maturity — and each interest check shrank too.

blocks.h: Name tells you the currency and the place
blocks.b:
- **Eurobond**: issued and sold **outside the country of its currency**; pays in that **foreign currency**.
- **Eurodollar bond**: issued **outside the U.S.**, pays **U.S. dollars**. Issuers: foreign or domestic corporations and governments (even municipalities) — but **never the U.S. Treasury**.
- **Yankee bond**: U.S.-dollar bond issued **by a non-U.S. entity inside the U.S. market** (Maple = Canadian-dollar version sold in Canada).

These issues skip **SEC registration** → cheaper to issue, less transparency, and higher yields to compensate for lower liquidity and political/country risk.

**Eurodollar bonds for a U.S. investor**: no currency risk, rated by U.S. agencies, often higher yield. Downsides: not SEC-registered, country risk, less liquid — and a **non-U.S. holder (a French investor) does bear currency risk**.

Created under Treasury Secretary Brady's 1989 plan (Mexico first, 1990) to convert defaulted Latin American bank loans into tradable bonds, with the IMF and World Bank as partners. Mostly **dollar-denominated**, 10–30 years, coupon, discount or zero. Safety rests on **collateral** — often U.S. Treasury zero-coupon bonds — so they are **safer and more liquid** than other emerging-market debt and let the country borrow more cheaply. Interest is **fully taxable**, and **no Brady bond carries a U.S. government guarantee**.

lessons.title: Getting your principal back: zeros, calls and conversions
lessons.objective: Explain zero-coupon bonds and STRIPS (including phantom income and volatility), how and why issuers call bonds, call protection, and the hybrid nature of convertibles with antidilution protection.

blocks.b:
A zero pays **no interest**; you buy at a deep **discount** and receive par at maturity. Pay $500 today, get $1,000 in 10 years.

- Always issued at a discount.
- **No reinvestment risk** — there are no coupons to reinvest; you lock in a yield for a chosen period.
- **More volatile** than coupon bonds of the same quality. Lowest coupon + longest maturity = most volatile.
- **Phantom income**: the IRS taxes the imputed interest each year (Form **1099-OID**) even though you receive nothing until maturity.

That tax quirk is why zeros suit **target-date goals** inside tax-sheltered wrappers — a child's college fund or a retirement plan. Corporate and municipal zeros add credit risk (nothing arrives for 20 years, so a failure at the end hurts). **Treasury STRIPS** have no credit risk — and are unrated because none is needed.

A **call feature** lets the **issuer** repay early. It is used when **rates have fallen**: issue new, cheaper bonds and retire the old high-coupon ones — **refunding**, the corporate version of refinancing a mortgage. Early calls usually pay a **premium** over par. After the final tender date, interest stops and any conversion right dies.

Issuers do **not** call bonds trading at a discount — buying them back in the open market is cheaper.

**Call protection** = the years before the first permitted call. **Noncallable** is the best protection an investor can have.

Investors can also end a bond early by **converting** (their choice, unlike a call). A convertible debenture is a hybrid:
- **Downside protection** — you are a creditor; interest and principal are owed, and the bond trades on its yield if the stock collapses. Less volatile than the stock.
- **Upside** — the bond rises with the common once the stock clears the conversion price, which softens interest-rate risk.
- **Costs** — a lower coupon than nonconvertibles, and the bond may be **called before you convert**.

Some allocators classify convertibles as **equity**.

**Antidilution**: on a stock split or stock dividend the conversion ratio adjusts (a bond convertible into 20 shares becomes 40 after a 2-for-1 split; the conversion price halves) so your conversion power is unchanged.

lessons.title: The money market and cash in the bank
lessons.objective: Characterize money market instruments (T-bills, jumbo CDs, commercial paper, Eurodollars), note the LIBOR-to-SOFR change, and compare demand deposits and bank CDs including why they have no interest-rate risk.

blocks.b:
The **money market** trades short-term loanable funds: instruments maturing in **one year or less** (most under six months). The **buyer is the lender**; the seller is the borrower. Nearly all are issued at a **discount** (paying coupons on a 90-day note isn't worth the bother), and all are **low risk** — though commercial paper is not quite a T-bill.

Why hold them: **liquidity**, **safety**, the right place for money needed soon. The costs: **low returns** (not a long-term core holding) and **fluctuating income** as maturing principal is reinvested at new rates.

- **T-bills** — the bellwether; plus Treasury notes/bonds in their last year.
- **Negotiable (jumbo) CDs** — **unsecured** bank time deposits of **$100,000+** (often $1 million+), tradable before maturity, **no prepayment penalty**, FDIC-insured up to **$250,000**. The one money market instrument **issued at par that pays periodic (semiannual) interest**.
- **Commercial paper** — short-term **unsecured** corporate notes (finance companies especially) for working capital, issued at a discount; exempt from registration when the maturity is **270 days or less**.
- **Eurodollars** — U.S. dollars deposited in banks **outside the U.S.** (Euroyen = yen outside Japan); overnight to 180 days; banks lend them to each other like fed funds.

blocks.h: Updated since the book: LIBOR is gone
blocks.b: The book calls **LIBOR** (London Interbank Offered Rate — a daily London bank survey across 15 periods and several currencies) the most widely used short-term benchmark and notes it was due to end June 30, 2023. It did end. The main U.S. replacement is **SOFR**, the **Secured Overnight Financing Rate**: the cost of borrowing cash **overnight, collateralized by Treasury securities**, published by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. If a question names LIBOR, it was set in **London**; the current overnight Treasury-secured benchmark is **SOFR**. (External source: NY Fed / ARRC transition.)

Bank money is **FDIC-insured** up to legal limits.
- **Demand deposit account (DDA)** — the legal term for a **checking** account (today also savings and bank money market *accounts* — but **not money market mutual funds**, which are securities). Withdraw any time; safe; low return; short-term money.
- **Bank (nonnegotiable) CDs** — as little as $500, 3 months to 5 years, early-withdrawal **penalty**, cannot be sold, only redeemed.

Exam rules: **capital preservation with no risk → insured bank CD**. Time deposits have **no interest-rate risk** because they don't trade — their value never fluctuates. They are liquid, though less than a DDA. What they do have: **purchasing-power risk** and low yields, so keep them a small part of a long-term plan.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes bond interest from stock dividends?
options: Both are paid at the discretion of the board of directors.
Interest is a contractual obligation deductible by a corporate issuer; dividends are discretionary and paid from after-tax income.
Dividends are a contractual obligation; interest may be skipped in poor years.
Interest is paid from after-tax income; dividends are a pre-tax expense.
questions.explanation: Interest must be paid as scheduled (default can lead to bankruptcy) and is a pre-tax expense for a corporation. Dividends are declared at the board's discretion out of after-tax income.
why: Only dividends are discretionary.
Reversed.
Reversed — interest is the deductible item.

questions.stem: The document that states the issuer's obligation to repay principal on a specific date, pay a specified rate of interest, and describes any collateral is the
questions.explanation: The indenture (deed of trust) is the contract between issuer and bondholders containing all the terms of the loan.
why: A prospectus discloses an offering; it is not the loan contract.
A debenture is a type of unsecured bond, not the contract.
Rating agencies issue opinions on quality, not contracts.

questions.stem: If market interest rates rise after a bond is issued, which of the following is TRUE of that outstanding bond?
questions.explanation: Prices of outstanding debt move inversely to market interest rates. Par value, coupon, and maturity are fixed by the indenture.
why: Par is fixed for the life of the bond.
Coupon payments never change with market rates.
Maturity is fixed.

questions.stem: An investor sells a corporate bond two months after its last semiannual interest payment. Regarding the interest that accrued during those two months,
options: the issuer pays it to the seller on the sale date.
the buyer pays it to the seller as part of the purchase, then collects the full next coupon.
it is forfeited by the seller.
the buyer and seller each receive half of the next coupon from the issuer.
questions.explanation: Bonds trade 'and interest': the buyer pays the price plus accrued interest to the seller and receives the entire next payment from the issuer.
why: The issuer pays only on scheduled dates, to the holder of record.
Accrued interest is compensated through the trade price.
The issuer pays the full coupon to the new owner only.

questions.stem: Moody's four investment-grade rating categories, from highest to lowest, are
questions.explanation: Moody's investment-grade categories are Aaa, Aa, A and Baa. Ba and below are speculative. AAA/AA/A/BBB is the S&P scale.
why: That is Standard & Poor's notation.
Ba is speculative, not investment grade.
Omits Aaa and includes speculative Ba.

questions.stem: A bank trust department may purchase only investment-grade bonds. Which of the following S&P-rated bonds is the LOWEST rating it could buy?
questions.explanation: Investment grade is the top four categories: AAA, AA, A and BBB. BB is the highest speculative grade.
why: A is investment grade but not the lowest permitted.
BB is speculative (high yield).
B is speculative.

questions.stem: Compared with investment-grade bonds, high-yield bonds generally
options: have lower default risk and lower volatility.
are the only bonds fiduciaries may purchase.
offer higher returns to compensate for greater default risk and price volatility.
carry a mortgage on the issuer's property.
questions.explanation: Lower-rated bonds must pay more to attract lenders (risk–reward). They are more volatile and more prone to price erosion in slow economies.
why: High-yield bonds have higher default risk and volatility.
Fiduciaries are generally limited to investment grade.
Collateral is unrelated to the high-yield classification; raters consider collateral among all factors.

questions.stem: A customer buys a U.S. Treasury bond quoted at 98.24. Ignoring commissions and accrued interest, the price paid is
why: Treats .24 as hundredths; it is 24/32.
Rounds incorrectly; 24/32 is $7.50, not $10.
Misreads the quote entirely.

questions.stem: A corporate bond is quoted at 96 3/8. Its dollar price is
why: Treats the fraction as cents.
Uses 7/8 instead of 3/8.
Arithmetic error.

questions.stem: A newspaper listing shows 'KLM 6s39 @ 94'. This means the KLM bond
options: pays $60 per year, matures in 2039, and is priced at $940.
pays 6% semiannually ($120 per year), matures in 2039, and is priced at $94.
pays $6 per year, has 39 years to maturity, and yields 9.4%.
pays $60 per year, matures in 2039, and trades at a premium of $94 over par.
questions.explanation: 6s = 6% coupon ($60 annually, $30 twice a year); 39 = maturity 2039; 94 = 94% of par = $940. The 's' is a separator.
why: 6% is the annual rate; the price is $940 not $94.
The coupon is a percentage of $1,000; 39 is a year, not years remaining.
94 is below par — a discount.

questions.stem: A convertible debenture is convertible at $40 per share and is currently trading at $1,100. The parity price of the common stock is
questions.explanation: Conversion ratio = $1,000 ÷ $40 = 25 shares. Parity stock price = $1,100 ÷ 25 = $44 (or: the bond is 10% above par, so 40 × 1.10 = 44).
why: Divides by 40 shares, an incorrect ratio.
That is the conversion price, not parity at $1,100.
Applies 10% twice.

questions.stem: A debenture is convertible into common stock at $25. If the common is trading at $22, the parity price of the debenture is
questions.explanation: Ratio = $1,000 ÷ $25 = 40 shares. Parity bond price = 40 × $22 = $880 (stock is 12% below the conversion price, so bond parity is 12% below par).
why: Parity equals par only when the stock trades at the conversion price.
Adds 12% instead of subtracting.
Uses 100 shares.

questions.stem: The JRP 5s of '41 are trading at 125 and are convertible at $50. Into how many shares does each bond convert?
questions.explanation: Conversion ratio is fixed by the indenture: $1,000 par ÷ $50 conversion price = 20 shares. The current market price is irrelevant.
why: Divides the market price ($1,250) by $50 — a common trap.
Uses $25.
Confuses the conversion price with the share count.

questions.stem: A 7% corporate bond is trading at 87 1/2. Its current yield is approximately
questions.explanation: Current yield = annual interest ÷ market price = $70 ÷ $875 = 8%.
why: Multiplies instead of divides.
That is the nominal yield; a discount bond's CY exceeds its coupon.
Confuses the price with the yield.

questions.stem: A bond with a 6% coupon that pays interest semiannually will pay the holder
questions.explanation: Coupon rates are annual: 6% of $1,000 = $60 per year, delivered as two $30 payments.
why: That would be a 12% bond.
Interest is paid semiannually.
That would be a 12% annual payer.

questions.stem: A bond with a 5% coupon is currently yielding 4.2%. The bond must be trading at
questions.explanation: A yield below the coupon rate means the investor paid more than par — pay more, get less — so the bond is at a premium.
why: A discount produces a yield above the coupon.
At par, yield equals the coupon.
The call price is not implied by yield alone.

questions.stem: For a bond purchased at a discount and held to maturity, which ranking of yields from lowest to highest is correct?
options: Yield to maturity, current yield, nominal yield
Nominal yield, current yield, yield to maturity
Current yield, nominal yield, yield to maturity
Yield to maturity, nominal yield, current yield
questions.explanation: On a discount bond the gain to par lifts YTM above CY, and CY (interest ÷ lower price) is above the coupon rate: nominal < CY < YTM (< YTC).
why: That is the premium-bond order, reversed.
CY exceeds nominal on a discount bond.
YTM is the highest of the three on a discount bond.

questions.stem: A client is considering a callable bond trading at 108. Which yield should the adviser emphasize as the most conservative measure of return?
questions.explanation: On a premium bond, yield to call is the lowest yield because the premium loss is accelerated to the call date; it is the worst case the investor should evaluate.
why: Nominal is the highest yield on a premium bond.
CY ignores the loss of the premium.
YTM spreads the loss to maturity; a call shortens that period.

questions.stem: If a bond's yield to maturity equals its current yield, the bond is trading at
options: a price that cannot be determined.
questions.explanation: Only at par is there no gain or loss at maturity, so YTM, CY and nominal yield are all equal.
why: At a discount, YTM > CY.
At a premium, YTM < CY.
Equal YTM and CY determines par.

questions.stem: An investor buys an 8% bond at 90 with 10 years to maturity. Using the approximation method, the yield to maturity is closest to
questions.explanation: Annual interest $80 + ($100 discount ÷ 10 years) = $90; average price = ($900 + $1,000) ÷ 2 = $950; $90 ÷ $950 ≈ 9.47%.
why: That is the nominal yield.
That is the current yield ($80 ÷ $900).
Ignores the averaging of price.

questions.stem: Which Treasury security is issued without a stated interest rate?
questions.explanation: T-bills are issued at a discount and pay no coupon; the return is the difference between the discounted price and par. Notes, bonds and TIPS all carry stated rates.
why: Notes pay semiannual interest at a stated rate.
Bonds pay semiannual interest at a stated rate.
TIPS have a fixed stated rate applied to adjusted principal.

questions.stem: This week's 13-week T-bill auction produced a yield of 3.10%, down from 3.35% last week. The best interpretation is that
options: this week's buyers paid less than last week's buyers.
this week's buyers paid more than last week's buyers.
the Treasury raised the coupon rate.
questions.explanation: T-bills are sold at a discount; a lower yield means a higher price was paid, reflecting strong demand.
why: Lower yield means higher price.
T-bills have no coupon.
Falling yields indicate rising demand.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of U.S. Treasury notes?
questions.explanation: Treasury notes and bonds are noncallable. They have intermediate maturities, pay semiannual interest, mature at par, and exist only as book entries.
why: Notes run 2, 3, 5, 7 and 10 years.
Notes pay interest twice a year.
All Treasuries are book entry.

questions.stem: Regarding Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, which statement is correct?
options: The coupon rate is adjusted semiannually for changes in the CPI.
The principal is adjusted semiannually for changes in the CPI, and the fixed rate is applied to the adjusted principal.
Increases in principal are exempt from federal income tax until maturity.
TIPS pay a higher coupon than conventional Treasuries of the same maturity.
questions.explanation: TIPS keep a fixed rate; the principal moves with the CPI, so interest payments rise and fall with inflation. Principal increases are federally taxable in the year they occur.
why: The rate is fixed; the principal adjusts.
Upward adjustments are taxable annually (phantom income).
TIPS pay a lower coupon because of the inflation adjustment.

questions.stem: A retiree wants periodic interest, safety of principal, and protection against loss of purchasing power. The most suitable recommendation is
questions.explanation: TIPS are government-guaranteed, pay semiannual interest, and adjust principal for inflation.
why: STRIPS pay no periodic interest and offer no inflation adjustment.
GNMAs carry prepayment risk and no inflation protection.
Zeros pay nothing until maturity and add credit risk.

questions.stem: Which of the following is TRUE of Ginnie Mae pass-through certificates?
options: They are moral obligations of the U.S. government.
They pay interest and principal monthly and are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government.
Their interest is exempt from state and local income tax.
They are backed by pools of conventional, uninsured mortgages.
questions.explanation: GNMA is a government corporation; its certificates carry the direct government guarantee, represent FHA/VA mortgage pools, and pass through monthly payments of interest plus principal, taxable at all levels.
why: That describes GSEs such as Fannie Mae; GNMA is directly guaranteed.
GNMA interest is taxable federally, state and locally.
The pools are FHA-insured or VA-guaranteed mortgages.

questions.stem: Mortgage-backed securities expose investors to prepayment risk primarily because
options: issuers call the securities when rates rise.
homeowners refinance when interest rates fall, returning principal early to be reinvested at lower rates.
the government guarantee expires after 10 years.
questions.explanation: Falling rates trigger refinancing; principal flows back to investors sooner than expected and must be reinvested at the lower prevailing rates — a form of reinvestment risk.
why: Prepayments come from borrowers, and when rates fall, not rise.
No such expiration exists.
Mortgage payments are monthly.

questions.stem: Which of the following debt securities is NOT backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government?
questions.explanation: Fannie Mae is a government-sponsored enterprise whose debt is a moral obligation only. Treasuries and GNMA securities carry the direct guarantee.
why: TIPS are Treasury obligations.
GNMA is a wholly owned government corporation with full backing.
Treasury bonds are direct obligations.

questions.stem: An airline finances new aircraft with debt secured by the planes themselves, with title held by a trustee until the loan is repaid. This security is
questions.explanation: Equipment trust certificates finance rolling stock, locomotives and aircraft; the trustee holds title until the debt is paid.
why: Mortgage bonds are secured by real estate.
Collateral trust bonds are secured by securities held in trust.
A debenture is unsecured.

questions.stem: A corporation with little real estate or equipment wishes to issue secured debt. It could pledge
options: marketable securities it owns, deposited in trust.
a guarantee from its parent company.
future revenues from a toll facility.
questions.explanation: A collateral trust bond is secured by marketable securities placed in trust. General credit backs a debenture; a parent's promise makes a guaranteed bond; toll revenues back municipal revenue bonds.
why: That backs an unsecured debenture.
A guaranteed bond is not secured by the issuer's assets.
That describes a municipal revenue bond.

questions.stem: In a corporate liquidation, which of the following is paid immediately AFTER the general (unsecured) creditors?
questions.explanation: Priority: secured creditors → general creditors (debentures) → subordinated debt → preferred → common.
why: Secured creditors are paid first.
Preferred follows all debt, including subordinated.
Common is last.

questions.stem: Which statement about a guaranteed corporate bond is correct?
options: It is secured by a pledge of the issuer's real property.
Its safety depends on the financial strength of the guarantor, a company other than the issuer.
It ranks ahead of mortgage bonds in liquidation.
It is guaranteed by the U.S. government.
questions.explanation: A guaranteed bond carries a promise from another corporation (often a parent) to pay interest, or interest and principal; it is only as good as that guarantor.
why: No asset of the issuer is pledged.
Secured bonds rank ahead.
The guarantee is corporate, not governmental.

questions.stem: A prospectus describes a corporation's outstanding 'senior bonds.' These are most likely
options: secured bonds such as mortgage or collateral trust bonds.
questions.explanation: Senior bonds are those with priority over unsecured creditors — mortgage bonds, collateral trust bonds, equipment trust certificates.
why: Subordinated debt is junior to other creditors.
Preferred is a senior security relative to common, but it is stock, not a bond.
Commercial paper is short-term unsecured debt.

questions.stem: A bond whose interest and principal are paid from the earnings of a municipal water and sewer system is
questions.explanation: Revenue bonds are payable from the earnings of a revenue-producing facility such as a water, sewer or electric system, toll bridge or airport.
why: GOs are backed by taxing power.
Treasuries are federal.
Collateral trust bonds are corporate, backed by securities.

questions.stem: Compared with a general obligation bond from the same issuer, a revenue bond typically
options: is backed by unlimited ad valorem taxes.
offers a higher yield because facility revenues are less certain than tax collections.
has a lower yield because of its superior security.
is exempt from federal tax while the GO is not.
questions.explanation: Taxes are more secure than project revenues, so revenue bonds must pay more.
why: Ad valorem taxes back GOs.
Revenue bonds are less secure, not more.
Both are generally federally tax-exempt.

questions.stem: An investor in the 32% federal tax bracket is offered a municipal bond at par with a 3.4% coupon. The tax-equivalent yield is
why: Multiplies by (1 − 0.32) — that converts a taxable yield to tax-free, the wrong direction.
Divides by 0.76 (uses a 24% bracket).
Divides by the bracket instead of its complement.

questions.stem: A corporate bond yields 6%. For an investor in the 35% bracket, a municipal bond would need to yield at least what to be equivalent after tax?
questions.explanation: The taxable bond nets 6% × (1 − 0.35) = 3.9%, so a 3.9% tax-free yield is equivalent.
why: 2.1% is the tax, not the after-tax yield.
Ignores taxes.
That is the TEY of a 6% muni, the reverse question.

questions.stem: A client in the 24% federal bracket can buy, at par and of similar quality: a 4.0% Treasury note, a 3.3% municipal bond, or a 4.4% corporate bond. Ranking by after-tax yield (highest first):
questions.explanation: After federal tax: corporate 4.4 × 0.76 = 3.34%; municipal 3.3% (tax-free); Treasury 4.0 × 0.76 = 3.04%. Corporate edges the muni at this low bracket.
why: The muni (3.3%) beats the Treasury (3.04%).
At 24%, the corporate's 3.34% beats the muni's 3.3%.
The Treasury is lowest.

questions.stem: A bond issued and sold outside the United States by a German corporation, with principal and interest paid in U.S. dollars, is
questions.explanation: Eurodollar bonds are dollar-denominated bonds issued outside the U.S. A Yankee bond would be sold inside the U.S. market; a Eurobond pays in a foreign currency.
why: It pays dollars, not a foreign currency.
Yankee bonds are issued in the U.S. market.
Brady bonds are restructured emerging-market sovereign debt.

questions.stem: All of the following are advantages of Eurodollar bonds to a U.S. investor EXCEPT
options: registration with the SEC providing full transparency.
potentially higher yields than domestic bonds of the same issuer.
questions.explanation: Eurodollar bonds are not registered with the SEC — that lowers issuance cost but reduces transparency, a disadvantage.
why: Dollar denomination removes currency risk for U.S. holders.
They are rated by U.S. agencies.
Higher yields compensate for lower liquidity and country risk.

questions.stem: Which statement about Brady bonds is correct?
options: They are guaranteed by the U.S. Treasury.
Their interest is exempt from U.S. federal income tax.
Their safety rests largely on pledged collateral, often U.S. Treasury zero-coupon bonds.
They are denominated only in the issuing country's currency.
questions.explanation: Brady bonds restructured defaulted emerging-market loans into mostly dollar-denominated bonds collateralized by Treasury zeros; interest is fully taxable and there is no U.S. guarantee.
why: No Brady bond carries a U.S. government guarantee.
Interest is fully taxable to U.S. investors.
Most are denominated in U.S. dollars.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about zero-coupon bonds is NOT true?
options: They are issued at a discount from par.
They are subject to reinvestment risk on their semiannual payments.
Holders may owe tax annually on imputed interest.
They are more volatile than coupon bonds of similar quality and maturity.
questions.explanation: Zeros make no periodic payments, so there is nothing to reinvest — no reinvestment risk. The other statements are true (phantom income via 1099-OID; higher volatility).
why: True — always issued at a discount.
True — the IRS taxes accreted interest yearly.
True — low coupon and long maturity maximize volatility.

questions.stem: A client wants to set aside a lump sum today that will grow to a known amount in 15 years for a child's education, with the greatest safety. The best choice is
questions.explanation: A Treasury STRIP provides a locked-in amount at maturity with no credit risk; even AAA corporates and municipals carry some default risk over 15 years.
why: Corporate zeros add credit risk with nothing received until maturity.
High-yield bonds are the least safe.
Municipal zeros carry more credit risk than Treasuries.

questions.stem: An issuer is most likely to exercise the call feature on its bonds when
options: interest rates have risen and the bonds trade at a discount.
interest rates have fallen and the bonds trade at a premium.
the bonds are about to mature.
the bonds' rating has been downgraded.
questions.explanation: Calls (refunding) make sense when the issuer can borrow more cheaply — after rates fall. When rates have risen, buying discounted bonds in the market is cheaper than calling.
why: Calling discount bonds would waste money.
Calls are early redemptions, not maturity.
A downgrade raises the issuer's borrowing cost, discouraging refunding.

questions.stem: Which of the following gives a bondholder the greatest protection against early redemption?
questions.explanation: A noncallable bond cannot be redeemed early at all — the best call protection possible.
why: A premium compensates but does not prevent a call.
Protection expires after ten years.
A sinking fund retires debt; it is not call protection.

questions.stem: An investor holds a debenture convertible into 25 shares. The issuer declares a 5-for-1 stock split. Under standard antidilution provisions, the debenture becomes convertible into
options: the same dollar value of shares at the holder's option.
questions.explanation: Antidilution adjusts the conversion ratio for splits and stock dividends: 25 × 5 = 125 shares (the conversion price falls to one-fifth), preserving the holder's conversion power.
why: That would reduce conversion power.
Unchanged ratio would dilute the holder.
The adjustment is mechanical, not optional.

questions.stem: Which money market instrument is issued at face value and pays periodic interest rather than being issued at a discount?
questions.explanation: Jumbo CDs are the exception: issued at par, paying interest (usually semiannually), unsecured, tradable, no prepayment penalty, FDIC-insured to $250,000.
why: T-bills are issued at a discount.
Commercial paper is issued at a discount.
Acceptances are discount instruments.

questions.stem: Commercial paper is exempt from registration under federal and state securities law provided that its maximum maturity does not exceed
questions.explanation: Commercial paper — short-term unsecured corporate notes for working capital — qualifies for the exemption when maturity is 270 days or less.
why: Too short; the limit is 270 days.
Too short.
One year is the money market cutoff, not the commercial paper exemption.

questions.stem: A business has $400,000 from an asset sale that it will need in about five months for a tax payment. The most appropriate recommendation is
questions.explanation: Money needed soon belongs in a safe, liquid money market instrument; nothing is safer than a T-bill.
why: Stocks could fall before the money is needed.
Long bonds carry interest-rate risk over five months.
A 5-year CD would impose an early-withdrawal penalty.

questions.source: external: NY Fed SOFR; LIBOR cessation 2023
questions.stem: The Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR), which replaced LIBOR as the primary U.S. short-term benchmark, measures
options: the rate at which London banks say they can borrow from each other.
the cost of borrowing cash overnight collateralized by U.S. Treasury securities.
the discount rate charged by the Federal Reserve.
questions.explanation: SOFR is based on actual overnight repurchase transactions secured by Treasuries and is published by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. LIBOR, the London bank-survey rate, was discontinued after June 2023.
why: That described LIBOR, now discontinued.
The discount rate is a Fed policy rate, not SOFR.
SOFR is an overnight secured rate, not a T-bill yield.

questions.stem: Which of the following has NO interest-rate risk?
options: An insured 2-year certificate of deposit at a local bank
questions.explanation: A nonnegotiable bank CD does not trade, so its value does not fluctuate with market rates. Tradable instruments — Treasuries, jumbo CDs, commercial paper — do fluctuate.
why: Treasury notes trade and fall in price when rates rise.
Jumbo CDs are negotiable and trade in the money market.
Commercial paper trades and is priced off market rates.

questions.stem: In banking terminology, a demand deposit account (DDA) is best described as
options: an account, such as a checking account, from which the customer may withdraw funds at any time.
a certificate of deposit with an early-withdrawal penalty.
a negotiable CD of $100,000 or more.
questions.explanation: DDA is the legal term for a checking account (now broadly including savings and bank money market accounts) — funds available on demand, insured, low return.
why: Money market mutual funds are securities, not bank deposits.
A CD is a time deposit.
That is a jumbo CD, a money market instrument.

questions.front: Indenture
questions.back: The bond contract (deed of trust): amount owed, maturity date, interest rate, collateral, other terms.

questions.front: Interest rates rise → outstanding bond prices __? Coupon payments __?
questions.back: Prices fall; coupon payments stay the same (and par never changes).

questions.front: Lowest investment-grade rating: S&P? Moody's?
questions.back: BBB (S&P) / Baa (Moody's). Top four categories are investment grade; BB/Ba and below are high yield.

questions.front: Treasury quote 104.16 = $?
questions.back: $1,045 — the .16 is 16/32 = 1/2 point = $5. Corporate 104 1/2 is the same price.

questions.front: Three convertible formulas
questions.back: Ratio = 1,000 ÷ conversion price. Parity stock = bond price ÷ ratio. Parity bond = ratio × stock price.

questions.front: Current yield formula
questions.back: Annual interest (or dividend) ÷ current market price. Discount → CY above coupon; premium → below.

questions.front: Yield ranking, lowest to highest — discount bond / premium bond
questions.back: Discount: nominal < CY < YTM < YTC. Premium: YTC < YTM < CY < nominal. Par: all equal.

questions.front: T-bill / T-note / T-bond maturities and interest
questions.back: Bills ≤ 52 weeks, discount, no coupon. Notes 2–10 yrs, bonds 10–30 yrs: semiannual interest, par at maturity, noncallable, book entry. 13-week bill = risk-free rate.

questions.front: TIPS: what adjusts, and how taxed?
questions.back: Principal adjusts with CPI semiannually; fixed rate × adjusted principal. Interest and principal increases federally taxable each year; exempt from state/local tax.

questions.front: GNMA vs. Fannie Mae: backing, payment frequency, tax
questions.back: GNMA: full faith & credit, monthly interest + principal. Fannie Mae (GSE): moral obligation, semiannual. Both taxable at all levels. Main risk of both: prepayment.

questions.front: Three types of secured corporate bonds and their collateral
questions.back: Mortgage bonds (real estate), equipment trust certificates (rolling stock/planes), collateral trust bonds (securities in trust).

questions.front: Liquidation priority
questions.back: Secured creditors → general/unsecured creditors (debentures) → subordinated debt → preferred stock → common stock.

questions.front: GO bond vs. revenue bond backing; which yields more?
questions.back: GO: full faith and credit, usually ad valorem (property) taxes. Revenue: earnings of a facility. Revenue bonds yield more.

questions.front: Tax-equivalent yield formula (both directions)
questions.back: TEY = muni yield ÷ (1 − bracket). Equivalent tax-free = taxable yield × (1 − bracket).

questions.front: Eurobond vs. Eurodollar bond vs. Yankee bond
questions.back: Eurobond: issued outside the currency's country, pays foreign currency. Eurodollar: issued outside U.S., pays USD (never issued by U.S. Treasury). Yankee: USD, non-U.S. issuer, sold in the U.S.

questions.front: Four facts about zero-coupon bonds
questions.back: Issued at a discount; no reinvestment risk; most volatile; phantom income taxed yearly (1099-OID). Safest zero = Treasury STRIP.

questions.front: When do issuers call bonds, and what is the best call protection?
questions.back: When rates have fallen (refunding). Best protection: a noncallable bond.

questions.front: Jumbo (negotiable) CD facts
questions.back: $100,000+; unsecured; issued at par, pays semiannual interest; no prepayment penalty; FDIC to $250,000; tradable; money market when ≤ 1 year.

questions.front: LIBOR vs. SOFR
questions.back: LIBOR: London interbank survey rate, discontinued 2023. SOFR: overnight rate secured by Treasuries, published by the NY Fed — the U.S. replacement.

questions.front: Which cash vehicle has no interest-rate risk and is the answer for 'capital preservation, no risk'?
questions.back: An insured bank CD / time deposit (does not trade, value never fluctuates). DDA = checking account.

terms.def: Interest earned since the last payment; paid by the bond buyer to the seller at settlement.
Property tax; the usual backing for municipal general obligation bonds.
Yield that accounts for the gain or loss to par at maturity; the bond's internal rate of return.
Years before an issuer may first call a bond; noncallable is the strongest.
Shares received per bond on conversion: $1,000 ÷ conversion price.
Unsecured corporate bond backed only by the issuer's general credit.
Dollar-denominated bond issued outside the U.S.; never issued by the U.S. Treasury.
The top four rating categories: BBB/Baa and above.
Price at which a convertible and the shares it converts into have equal value.
Taxable imputed interest on zero-coupon bonds (and TIPS principal increases) received only at maturity.
Risk that mortgage-backed principal returns early (refinancing when rates fall); a form of reinvestment risk.
Calling old bonds using proceeds of new, lower-coupon bonds.
Secured Overnight Financing Rate — Treasury-collateralized overnight borrowing rate that replaced LIBOR (external update).
Zero-coupon Treasuries (Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal of Securities); no credit risk.
Municipal yield ÷ (1 − tax bracket): the taxable yield needed to match a tax-free bond.
Dollar-denominated bond issued in the U.S. market by a non-U.S. entity.
